{#g1ki} # Discussion

{#oppb} In this present study, we examined the predictive value of SHR for the risk of one-year mortality among HF patients from MIMIC-IV database, regardless of the status of DM. Our findings demonstrate that a higher SHR is correlated with a higher risk of one-year mortality in patients with HF, irrespective of the presence of DM. Specifically, the adjusted hazard ratios suggest that an elevated SHR is associated with an 88.1% increased risk of one-year mortality in HF patients with DM and a 27.8% increased risk in those without DM. Additionally, we explore the effect of SHR on one-year mortality according to the AHF and CHF groups. Our results suggest that the predictive role of SHR for one-year all-cause mortality is consistent among both AHF and CHF patients. This consistent association across different subgroups underscores the robustness of SHR as a predictor for poor prognosis in HF. The Kaplan–Meier curves also show that higher SHR is associated with an elevated risk of one-year mortality in patients with HF, both in the DM and non-DM groups. The RCS curve shows a gradual increase in the probability of one-year mortality as the value of SHR increases for HF patients with DM. Similarly, for HF patients without DM, the RCS curve also demonstrates a comparable trend. Both curves suggest a negative correlation between SHR and survival probability in HF patients with and without DM.

ops.markdown: It is widely recognized that stress hyperglycemia is linked to an elevated risk of mortality and adverse clinical outcomes in critically ill patients [23, 32]. However, intensive glucose-lowering treatment may paradoxically increase the risk of death, making glucose management in critical illness challenging [33]; an international randomized controlled trial found that intensive glucose control increased ICU mortality, possibly through severe hypoglycemia [33]. A retrospective study of 45,000 critically ill patients found that without DM, a mean blood glucose level of 4.4 to 7.8 mmol/L was linked to lower mortality, whereas patients with DM tolerated higher levels: those with a mean blood glucose level of > 6.1 mmol/L had lower mortality than DM patients with a mean blood glucose level of 4.4 to 6.1 mmol/L [34]. Stress hyperglycemia generally indicates a more critical condition; in our study, the high SHR group was older, more often had ACS and CAD, and had higher white blood cell and lower hemoglobin levels, consistent with more severe disease. Therefore, managing HF patients with stress hyperglycemia requires both reasonable glycemic control and rigorous treatment of HF and co-existing conditions. SHR levels can also be influenced by sepsis, cerebrovascular and cardiovascular diseases, and other critical illnesses [35]; we therefore adjusted for these variables, but SHR should be interpreted cautiously, since nutritional status and other diseases may also affect it [36]. The current ESC guidelines recommend sodium-glucose transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for HF patients regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) once stable [37], and a further study suggests that SGLT2 inhibitors may protect the heart by inhibiting cardiomyocyte autophagy, improving survival in mice with MI and acute hyperglycemia [38]. Patients with HF and stress hyperglycemia may therefore derive greater benefit from SGLT2 inhibitors, although further research is required.
